result.summary: Alcinous and the Phaeacians send Ulysses home with more gifts, and he sleeps through the voyage and is laid on the shore of Ithaca. Neptune, angry, turns the returning Phaeacian ship to stone. Minerva meets Ulysses, reveals that he is home, helps him hide his treasure, and disguises him as a beggar to plan against the suitors.

scenes.title: Farewell feast and departure
scenes.summary: Alcinous arranges extra gifts, the Phaeacians feast, and Ulysses bids farewell and sails off asleep in the swift ship.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses's long-awaited homecoming depends on the escort being carried out.

scenes.title: Landing in the harbour of Phorcys
scenes.summary: The ship reaches Ithaca at dawn, and the crew lay the sleeping Ulysses on the sand with his gifts under the olive tree.
scenes.stakes: The gifts could be stolen before Ulysses wakes.

scenes.title: Neptune petrifies the Phaeacian ship
scenes.summary: Neptune complains to Jove and, with his advice, turns the ship to stone. Alcinous recalls the old prophecy and orders sacrifices.
scenes.stakes: The Phaeacians risk having their city buried under a mountain.

scenes.title: Ulysses wakes in a strange land
scenes.summary: Ulysses wakes in fog, does not recognise Ithaca, and despairs, then counts his treasure.
scenes.stakes: He fears he is in a hostile land and may lose his treasure.

scenes.title: Minerva reveals Ithaca
scenes.summary: Minerva, disguised as a shepherd, hears Ulysses's lying Cretan tale, then reveals herself and clears the mist so he sees Ithaca.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks mistrust and deception when he may in fact have an ally.

scenes.title: Plotting against the suitors
scenes.summary: They hide the treasure in the cave. Minerva plans revenge, disguises Ulysses as a beggar, sends him to the swineherd, and goes to fetch Telemachus.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses must defeat the suitors, who plan to kill Telemachus, and retake his house.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of the sea god as shaker of the earth.

notable_quotes.reason: Minerva teases Ulysses for his compulsive lying even at home.
Minerva and Ulysses acknowledge each other as masters of cunning.

analysis.text: Ulysses's return is not an ending: he must stay cautious and deceptive. Minerva's disguise prepares him to reclaim his house.
The Phaeacian escort reflects Greek guest-friendship (xenia), while Neptune's punishment shows divine anger over human acts.

legacy.text: The petrified Phaeacian ship became a famous image; Corfu's islet Pontikonisi is traditionally identified with it.

fun_facts.text: The two doors of the nymphs' cave, one for mortals and one for gods, were later given allegorical readings by Porphyry.

language_notes.text: A tripod is a three-legged bronze cauldron stand or vessel, a prized gift and measure of wealth in Homeric society.
"Levy of a general rate" means a tax on the whole community, like a local rate, so no single noble bears the cost.
"Child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" is Homer's fixed formula for sunrise, repeated throughout the poem.
A drink-offering (libation) was wine poured out to the gods before a departure or at a feast's close.
A hawser is a thick mooring rope; here it is tied to a pierced stone serving as a bollard on the shore.
"Curvetted" means leapt or bounded like a spirited horse, here describing the ship's prow rising over the waves.
The bright star heralding dawn is the morning star (Venus); Homer often marks time by it.
Phorcys is a sea god, called an 'old merman' here; the harbour is named for him.
Naiads are nymphs of fresh water, springs and streams.
Sea purple is cloth dyed with costly purple dye made from shellfish.
'So much way upon her' means the ship still had great forward momentum, so it slid up onto the beach.
'Nodded your head' refers to Jove's nod as a sign of binding promise: he had agreed Ulysses would return.
'Lord of the Earthquake' is a standard title of Neptune, god of the sea and earthquakes.
Scheria is the island of the Phaeacians.
'Bless my heart' is a mild exclamation of surprise, in this translator's Victorian idiom.
Smiting the thighs with the flat of the hands is a Homeric gesture of grief or dismay.
Jove protects suppliants and guests, so Ulysses appeals to him against the Phaeacians, who he thinks broke their promise.
"Coppers" here means bronze or copper vessels; in this translation, valuables such as tripods and cauldrons were treasure.
Embracing the knees was the formal gesture of a suppliant begging for protection.
"Vassal" is the translator's word for a subordinate serving a lord, here Idomeneus, king of Crete.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) was angry because Ulysses blinded his son, the Cyclops Polyphemus.
Phorcys was a sea god; Naiads are nymphs of springs and fresh water. A hecatomb was a large sacrifice, originally of a hundred oxen.
The Phaeacians are the seafaring people who gave Ulysses gifts and carried him home to Ithaca while he slept.
"Compass the destruction" is archaic for bring about or achieve the suitors' destruction.
"Lording it" means behaving like masters, acting arrogantly in another man's house.
Agamemnon was murdered on his return from Troy by his wife Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus. Ulysses fears a similar fate.
"Troy's fair diadem" refers to the city's crown-like walls and towers; Minerva helped the Greeks take Troy by the wooden horse stratagem.
"Bespatter" means to splash or soil; "substance" here means wealth or property.
"Blear" means to dim or make the eyes watery and sore; "unseemly" means unfit to look at.
The swineherd is Eumaeus, Ulysses' loyal servant. Raven's Rock and the fountain Arethusa are places on Ithaca.
A "wallet" is a beggar's bag; a "thong" is a leather strap.

context_notes.text: Jove (the Greek Zeus) is king of the gods and guardian of guests and suppliants, so a sacrifice to him suits a farewell.
Demodocus is the blind bard of the Phaeacians, who sang of Troy earlier in the Phaeacian episode.
Arete is Alcinous' queen, whom Ulysses was told to supplicate first; his farewell to her honours that advice.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) hates Ulysses for blinding his son, the Cyclops Polyphemus.
The Phaeacians descend from Neptune, which is why he feels personally slighted.
The Phaeacians were famed for giving safe sea escorts to strangers, which is why Neptune resents them.
Ulysses has just been landed asleep on Ithaca by the Phaeacians. Minerva (the Greek Athena) is his divine protector.
Pylos and Elis are regions of the Peloponnese in Greece. Phoenicians were famed seafaring traders, and Sidonia means Sidon, their city.
Minerva is goddess of wisdom and crafty strategy, which is why she values Ulysses' cunning as akin to her own.
Penelope has put off the suitors for years, notably with the shroud she wove by day and unpicked by night.
Telemachus, Ulysses' son, went to Menelaus at Lacedaemon (Sparta) to seek news of his father.
Minerva's wand is her tool for transformations; the beggar disguise lets Ulysses test his household unrecognized.

literary_notes.text: Ulysses' longing for sunset is compared to a tired ploughman's longing for supper, placing the hero's desire in everyday labour.
His deathlike sleep prepares for his waking in Ithaca, almost a rebirth, with no awareness of the landing.
The ship's speed is likened to a four-horse chariot under the whip, stressing the swift, magical passage home.
"Cunning as the gods" recalls Ulysses' defining trait, contrasting his cleverness with his helpless sleep and past suffering.
The two entrances, one human and one divine, mark the cave as a threshold between mortal and divine worlds.
Neptune's casual slap that turns a ship to stone shows divine power on a vast scale.
Alcinous recalls the old prophecy fulfilled, and his fear of the mountain looming over the city hints at later consequences.
The Phaeacians pray in fear while Ulysses, the cause of it all, wakes unaware on his own soil.
The fog hides Ulysses until he takes revenge, hinting at the coming conflict with the suitors.
Ulysses lies by instinct even on hearing good news, showing his habitual wiliness.
Minerva, herself disguised and deceiving, chides Ulysses for deceit, then admits they are alike.
The lifting of the mist stands for Ulysses' recognition of home and the end of his wandering.
Minerva says Penelope means the opposite of her encouraging messages; the reader sees her loyalty while the suitors are deceived.
Ulysses' claim he could fight three hundred men, with the goddess's help, stresses his confidence in divine aid.
The planned disguise, hidden even from wife and son, prepares for the later recognition scenes and the suitors' slaughter.
Minerva predicts that suitors will find graves, anticipating the coming vengeance.
